newsitem.title: USA: Stocks plunge; investors shift to bonds.
newsitem.headline: Stocks plunge; investors shift to bonds.

text.p: Stocks fell Thursday following a jump in long-term interest rates above the key 7 percent level, which boosted the attractiveness of bonds.

At 1 p.m. EST, the Dow Jones industrial average was down 70.24 points at 6,810.46. In the broader market, declining issues beat advances 2-1 on active New York Stock Exchange volume of 256 million shares.
The Nasdaq composite index was off 6.20 points at 1,262.88.
Bonds headed sharply lower, and their yields soared on stronger-than-expected February existing home sales.

The key 30-year Treasury bond was off more than a full point, and its yield shot up to 7.08 percent from 6.98 percent at Wednesday's close. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions. Yields above 7 percent tend to draw money away from stocks and into bonds.
"The data this morning sent a shock wave through markets," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer for First Albanmy Corp.
"It's a very troubling day on Wall Street," he said. "The real problem is the heavy selling which was set off in the bond market when the long bond yield topped 7 percent."

Existing home sales rose 9 percent last month to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 4.26 million, compared with a forecast 4.05 million, the National Association of Realtors said. The January rate was a revised 3.91 million.
"If you combine yesterday's durable goods number with the existing home sales numbers you are left with the impression that the economy is strengthening, not slowing," Johnson said.
Durable goods orders rose 1.5 percent in February vs. analysts' expectations for a drop of 0.4 percent after January's strong gain of 4.1 percent.
The unexpected February orders pickup suggested the economy's industrial sector remained vigorous and might be gaining momentum.

"Tactical asset allocators are much more likely to focus on the bond market with the yield above 7 percent than on stocks with the Dow at 6,800," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co. "This is going to be a problem for the stock market."
Analysts said they were surprised by such a sell-off coming ahead of the start of the three-day Easter holiday weekend.

Among the losers in the 30-stock Dow index, Procter & Gamble Co. was down 2-1/2 at 118-1/2, Merck & Co. lost 1 to 89-7/8, International Business Machines Corp. fell 1-7/8 to 138-3/4 and Boeing Co. was down 3-1/2 at 101-3/4.
Banking stocks also took a beating.
Citicorp was down 2-1/4 at 111-3/8, BankAmerica Corp. sank 3-1/2 to 105-3/4, Chase Manhattan Corp. was down 2-1/2 at 97-3/8 and Dow component J.P. Morgan & Co. was off 2-1/8 at 103-3/8.

"The 7 percent bond yield is a big number but the 7.15-7.20 percent range is more important. It looks as though we are on our way to that area," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd.

"Market participants have not adjusted to a continued upward bias in interest rates and an uncertain profit outlook," said Metz. "The real problem is that worldwide we have seen the period of maximum monetary ease. It won't get any better. If anything, rates will edge up from here."

Among special situations, Quaker Oats Co. was up 3/4 at 38-1/4 after it agreed to sell its Snapple premium beverage unit for $300 million to Triarc Cos., owner of rival Mistic beverages. Triarc was up 1 at 16-3/4.
